body.objective: Students will be able to identify hazards and follow safety procedures.
body.iCan: I can identify hazards and follow safety procedures.
successCriteria: I can identify hazards in a CTS lab or shop
I can choose and use the right personal protective equipment
I can follow and explain safety procedures
body.hook: In Canadian workplaces, young and new workers are injured on the job at higher rates than experienced workers, often in their first months. The skills that keep you safe in a CTS lab, like reading hazards, using protective equipment and following procedures, are the same ones that keep workers safe in kitchens, shops and studios.

vocabulary.definition: Anything that could cause harm, such as a hot surface, sharp blade or chemical.
How likely a hazard is to cause harm and how serious it could be.
Gear such as safety glasses, gloves and aprons that protects the worker.
A document describing the hazards and safe handling of a product.
The Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System, Canada's system for labelling hazardous products.
Confirmation that a student has been trained to use a tool or machine safely.

study.title: Hazard Hunt
study.question: How do I work safely in a CTS lab or shop?
study.passage:
Part 1, Hazard hunt (15 minutes): In pairs, walk through the CTS lab (foods lab, construction shop, design studio or computer lab) with a checklist. Record every hazard you find in four categories:
• Physical (sharp tools, moving parts, hot surfaces, tripping hazards, noise)
• Chemical (cleaning products, finishes, adhesives)
• Biological (raw meat, mould, unwashed hands)
• Ergonomic (poor posture, repetitive motion, heavy lifting)
Part 2, PPE match (10 minutes): Match tasks to PPE: cutting wood (safety glasses, hearing protection on power tools), using a chef's knife (cut-resistant technique, closed-toe shoes), handling a cleaning chemical (gloves, eye protection, check the SDS), soldering (safety glasses, ventilation).
Part 3, WHMIS symbols (10 minutes): Identify common WHMIS pictograms on real labels (flame, corrosion, exclamation mark, health hazard). Find the SDS for one product and record the first-aid measures.
Part 4, Procedure (10 minutes): Watch the teacher demonstrate one tool or appliance. Write the safe procedure in five steps, then demonstrate it back for a safety sign-off.
Your rights at work (Alberta Occupational Health and Safety): the right to know about hazards, the right to participate in health and safety, and the right to refuse dangerous work.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; worker rights summarized from Alberta Occupational Health and Safety.
steps: Hunt for hazards in four categories
Identify WHMIS pictograms and read an SDS
Write and demonstrate a safe procedure
discussion: Which hazards were easiest to miss?
Why is PPE the last line of defence, not the first?
What did the SDS tell you that the label didn't?
How do the three worker rights protect you at a part-time job?
study.product: Create a one-page safety guide for one CTS lab or shop: the top five hazards, PPE needed, two WHMIS symbols with meanings, a five-step procedure for one tool, and the three worker rights.

practice.a: Personal protective equipment such as safety glasses and gloves.
Canada's system for labelling hazardous products.
Confirmation you've been trained to use a tool safely.

practice.q: Give an example of a biological hazard.
Give an example of an ergonomic hazard.
practice.a: Poor posture (also repetitive motion, heavy lifting).
Right to know, right to participate and right to refuse dangerous work.

practice.q: What PPE is used when soldering?
Where do you find first-aid measures for a chemical?
Why is PPE the last line of defence?
practice.a: It's better to remove or guard the hazard first; PPE protects only if the others fail.

practice.q: Why are young workers at higher risk?
practice.a: Less experience and training, and hesitation to speak up.

practice.q: Why must you get a sign-off before using a machine?
practice.a: To show you can use it safely.

practice.q: How does risk differ from hazard?
practice.a: A hazard can cause harm; risk is how likely and how serious that harm is.

misconceptions: Thinking PPE alone makes a task safe
Thinking safety rules don't apply to quick jobs
Being afraid to report hazards or refuse unsafe work

items.q: List the four hazard categories with an example of each.

items.q: Name the three Alberta worker rights.
items.answer: Right to know, participate and refuse dangerous work.

items.q: Write a five-step safe procedure for one tool.

items.answer: Hazards, safe handling, storage and first-aid measures.
